opts: An error of omission where both sides of a transaction were not recorded at all
A compensating error where two errors cancel each other out
A partial omission of entry where only one side of a transaction is posted
An error of principle where the item is posted to the wrong type of account
questionBank.exp: The manual lists as an error revealed by the trial balance: 'Partial omission of entry - Posting only a single entry without a corresponding one i.e. entering only one side of a transaction.'

questionBank.q: In the general journal, what information is typically included in the 'Particulars' column?
opts: The date of the transaction and the sequential entry number
The accounts being debited and credited and a brief description
The amount of the transaction and the posting reference number
The customer or supplier name and the invoice reference number
questionBank.exp: The Particulars column of a journal entry includes the accounts being debited (listed first, typically indented) and credited, followed by a brief description of the transaction.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance shows debit totals of N500,000 and credit totals of N498,000. Which of the following actions is most appropriate?
opts: Prepare the financial statements with the N2,000 difference as a profit
Create a Suspense Account with a credit balance of N2,000 to balance the trial balance
Create a Suspense Account with a debit balance of N2,000 to balance the trial balance
Post an adjusting entry of N2,000 to the Income Summary account
questionBank.exp: When trial balance totals are not equal, the difference of N2,000 (debit exceeds credit) is inserted as a credit balance in a Suspense Account to make the totals equal. A debit balance in Suspense would make debits exceed credits even more. The correct treatment is to credit Suspense with N2,000.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps in the accounting cycle?
opts: Journal entries, Trial Balance, Financial Statements, Ledger Posting, Adjusting Entries
Transaction Analysis, Journal Entries, Ledger Posting, Trial Balance, Adjusting Entries, Financial Statements
Ledger Posting, Journal Entries, Trial Balance, Adjusting Entries, Financial Statements, Closing Entries
Financial Statements, Adjusting Entries, Trial Balance, Journal Entries, Transaction Analysis
questionBank.exp: The accounting cycle follows a logical sequence: Transactions are identified and analyzed, then recorded in journals, posted to ledgers, summarized in a trial balance, adjusted, and finally used to prepare financial statements.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of preparing a trial balance in the accounting cycle?
opts: To identify and correct all errors in the accounting records before preparing financial statements
To verify the arithmetical accuracy of ledger entries by ensuring debits equal credits
To provide a complete list of all transactions that occurred during the accounting period
To calculate the net profit or loss for the accounting period before adjustments
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The trial balance checks the arithmetic accuracy of the ledger entries.' It is a list of all account balances arranged in debit and credit columns to ensure they are equal.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance shows a debit balance of N15,000 in the bank account. What does this balance represent?
opts: An overdraft owed to the bank which is a liability of the company
A positive cash balance held by the company at the bank
An amount owed by the bank to the company for interest
A provision for future bank charges and fees to be paid
questionBank.exp: A debit balance in the bank account (which is an asset) indicates that the company has cash at the bank. A credit balance would indicate an overdraft (liability).

questionBank.q: Which of the following errors would NOT be revealed by the trial balance?
opts: An error where a transaction was recorded with unequal debits and credits
An error where a transaction was omitted entirely from the accounting records
An error where the wrong amount was posted to both debit and credit accounts
An error where a debit balance was extracted as a credit balance
questionBank.exp: The manual lists errors of omission as: 'no entry for a transaction has been made at all.' Since no entry was made, the trial balance would still balance and the error would not be revealed.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of posting journal entries to the general ledger?
opts: To provide a chronological record of all transactions for audit purposes
To summarize all transactions of the same type into a single account balance
To prepare the financial statements directly from the journal entries
To calculate the profit or loss for each individual transaction
questionBank.exp: Posting transfers information from journals to the general ledger, where each account's cumulative balance is maintained. The manual states: 'The general ledger contains a complete record of all accounts used by a company.'

questionBank.q: A business has a credit balance of N5,000 in its Accounts Payable ledger account. What does this balance indicate?
opts: The business has overpaid its suppliers and is owed a refund
The business owes N5,000 to its suppliers for goods purchased on credit
The business has paid N5,000 in advance to its suppliers
The business has received N5,000 in goods but not yet paid
questionBank.exp: Accounts Payable is a liability account with a normal credit balance. A credit balance of N5,000 indicates the company owes N5,000 to its suppliers for goods or services received on credit.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for opening balances when starting a new set of books?
opts: Opening entries are recorded in the general journal and then posted to the ledger
Opening balances are entered directly into the financial statements without journal entries
Opening balances are recorded in the cash book only and not in the general ledger
Opening balances are determined by the trial balance of the previous period
questionBank.exp: Opening entries are recorded in the general journal first, then posted to the ledger accounts. The manual lists 'Opening entries. These are the entries needed to open a new set of books' as a use of the General Journal.

questionBank.q: A trial balance that has equal debit and credit totals guarantees that the financial statements will be accurate. Is this statement correct?
opts: Yes, because equal totals indicate all transactions have been recorded correctly
No, because certain errors like complete omission or wrong classification are not revealed
Yes, because the trial balance is the final check before preparing financial statements
No, because the trial balance does not verify that the correct accounts were used
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'However, the trial balance does not reveal all types of errors.' Errors like complete omission, errors of principle, and compensating errors are not revealed even when debits equal credits.

questionBank.q: When preparing a trial balance, accounts with debit balances typically include which of the following?
opts: Assets, expenses, and drawings accounts
Liabilities, revenue, and capital accounts
Assets, liabilities, and revenue accounts
Expenses, revenue, and drawings accounts
questionBank.exp: Asset accounts, expense accounts, and drawings accounts normally have debit balances. Liability, revenue, and capital accounts normally have credit balances.

questionBank.q: Which of the following transactions would be recorded in the Cash Book?
opts: The purchase of inventory on credit from a supplier
The sale of goods on credit to a customer
The payment of salaries by cheque to employees
The depreciation of equipment for the accounting period
questionBank.exp: The Cash Book is used for cash and cheque receipts and payments. The manual defines it as: 'Cash Book - for cash and cheque receipts and payments.'

questionBank.q: In the accounting cycle, what is the relationship between the journal and the ledger?
opts: The journal is prepared after the ledger to verify the accuracy of posting
The journal is the book of original entry and the ledger is the book of final entry
The journal and ledger serve the same purpose and can be used interchangeably
The journal is prepared annually while the ledger is prepared monthly
questionBank.exp: Transactions are first recorded in the journal (book of original entry) and then posted to the ledger (book of final entry) where account balances are accumulated.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct format for a journal entry with two debits and one credit?
opts: Debit Account A N100, Debit Account B N100, and Credit Account C N100
Debit Account A N100, Credit Account B N100, and Credit Account C N100
Debit Account A N100, Debit Account B N100, and Credit Account C N200
Debit Account A N100, Credit Account B N100, and Credit Account C N200
questionBank.exp: In a compound journal entry, the total debits must equal the total credits. For two debits of N100 each, the total debits are N200, so the credit side must also be N200.

questionBank.q: Which of the following errors would cause the trial balance to have unequal debit and credit totals?
opts: An error of commission where the amount is posted to the wrong personal account
A compensating error where two errors cancel each other out
An error of omission where the transaction was completely missed
A partial reversal of entry where one side of the entry is reversed
questionBank.exp: The manual lists as an error revealed by the trial balance: 'Partial reversal of entry - When the double entries of a transaction is posted to the same sides of the different ledgers or respective accounts.'

questionBank.q: Which account in the general ledger would typically have a credit balance?
opts: Furniture and Fittings which is a tangible asset used in operations
Accounts Receivable which represents amounts owed by customers
Sales Revenue which represents income earned by the business
Rent Expense which represents costs incurred for premises
questionBank.exp: Revenue accounts like Sales Revenue have normal credit balances. Assets (Furniture, Accounts Receivable) have debit balances, and Expenses (Rent) have debit balances.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of using specialized journals like the Sales Journal and Purchases Journal?
opts: To reduce the workload by grouping similar types of transactions together
To ensure that all transactions are recorded in the general ledger
To provide additional detail for audit and regulatory compliance
To separate cash transactions from credit transactions for reporting
questionBank.exp: Specialized journals allow businesses to record large volumes of similar transactions (like credit sales or credit purchases) efficiently. The manual identifies these as 'books of original entry' for similar transactions.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance shows total debits of N250,000 and total credits of N250,000. What conclusion can be drawn from this?
opts: The accounting records are completely error-free and accurate
The ledger accounts are arithmetically balanced but may still contain errors
The financial statements are ready to be prepared without further adjustments
All transactions have been correctly classified and recorded
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The trial balance checks the arithmetic accuracy of the ledger entries. However, the trial balance does not reveal all types of errors.' Equal totals indicate arithmetic accuracy but do not guarantee the absence of errors like omission or misclassification.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a use of the General Journal as identified in the manual?
opts: Recording the purchase of a fixed asset on credit
Recording the write-off of a bad debt from a customer
Recording the correction of errors in the ledger accounts
Recording all cash sales made by the business during the period
questionBank.exp: Cash sales are typically recorded in the Cash Book, not the General Journal. The General Journal is used for non-routine transactions such as asset purchases on credit, bad debt write-offs, and error corrections.

questionBank.q: In the accounting cycle, what is the purpose of the closing entries?
opts: To reset the balances of temporary accounts to zero for the next period
To calculate the net profit or loss for the accounting period
To prepare the trial balance for the start of the next period
To record all adjusting entries for the accounting period
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'A closing entry is a journal entry that is made at the end of an accounting period to transfer balances from a temporary account to a permanent account.' This resets temporary accounts to zero for the next period.

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for the balance of the Bank account when preparing a trial balance?
opts: A credit balance indicates cash in hand, which is an asset of the business
A debit balance indicates cash in hand, which is an asset of the business
A debit balance indicates an overdraft, which is a liability of the business
A credit balance indicates the business owes money to the customer
questionBank.exp: A debit balance in the Bank account represents cash at bank, which is an asset. A credit balance would represent a bank overdraft, which is a liability.

questionBank.q: A company purchases goods for resale and pays with a cheque. Which journal would be used to record this transaction?
opts: The Purchases Journal since it involves the purchase of inventory
The Cash Book since the payment was made by cheque
The Sales Journal since it involves goods for resale
The General Journal since it is a non-routine transaction
questionBank.exp: The Cash Book is used for cash and cheque receipts and payments. Since the payment was made by cheque, it would be recorded in the Cash Book.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the accounting cycle and the preparation of financial statements?
opts: Financial statements are prepared at the beginning of the accounting cycle
Financial statements are the final output of the accounting cycle
Financial statements replace the need for the accounting cycle
Financial statements are prepared before adjusting entries are made
questionBank.exp: The accounting cycle is a series of steps that begins with transaction analysis and ends with the preparation of financial statements. The manual's diagram shows financial statements as one of the final steps in the cycle.

questionBank.q: A trial balance shows a debit balance of N12,000 in the Wages account. What does this balance represent?
opts: Wages paid in advance by employees for future work
The total wages expense incurred by the business during the period
Wages owed by the business to employees at the end of the period
Wages charged to customers for services provided
questionBank.exp: Wages is an expense account with a normal debit balance. A debit balance of N12,000 represents the total wages expense incurred during the accounting period.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the 'Description' or 'Narration' in a journal entry?
opts: To provide a brief explanation of the transaction for future reference
To calculate the tax implications of the transaction being recorded
To identify the person who authorized the transaction
To determine which accounts should be debited and credited
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Provide a brief description of the transaction for future reference.' The narration explains the nature and purpose of the transaction.

questionBank.q: When analyzing a transaction using the six-step process, what is the final step?
opts: Determining the type of each account involved in the transaction
Deciding whether each account should be debited or credited
Determining the monetary amount of the transaction
Recording the transaction in the journal with the correct amounts
questionBank.exp: The manual's six-step process concludes with: 'For each account the monetary amount is [X].' Step 6 is determining the amount, after which the transaction can be recorded in the journal.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance shows a credit balance of N20,000 in the Loan Payable account. What does this balance indicate?
opts: The company has repaid N20,000 of its loan during the period
The company owes N20,000 on its loan balance at period end
The company has received N20,000 in new loan proceeds
The company has paid N20,000 in interest on its loan
questionBank.exp: Loan Payable is a liability account with a normal credit balance. A credit balance of N20,000 indicates the company has an outstanding loan balance of N20,000.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence for recording transactions in the accounting system?
opts: Source Documents, Ledger, Journal, Trial Balance, Financial Statements
Source Documents, Journal, Ledger, Trial Balance, Financial Statements
Source Documents, Trial Balance, Journal, Ledger, Financial Statements
Journal, Source Documents, Ledger, Trial Balance, Financial Statements
questionBank.exp: The correct sequence is: Source Documents (evidence) → Journal (book of original entry) → Ledger (book of final entry) → Trial Balance → Financial Statements.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of a compensating error that may leave a trial balance balanced?
opts: A transaction is completely omitted from both the debit and credit records
One account is overstated by ₦500 and another account is understated by ₦500, offsetting each other
A debit and its corresponding credit are both recorded as ₦100 instead of ₦1,000
A purchase is posted to the correct supplier account but the wrong expense account
questionBank.exp: A compensating error occurs when two or more errors offset each other in their effect on the trial-balance totals. Recording both sides of one transaction at the same incorrect amount is an error of original entry, not a compensating error.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the Income Summary account in the closing process?
opts: To summarize all income and expenses before transferring to the capital account
To calculate the total assets and liabilities of the business at period end
To record all adjusting entries for the accounting period
To serve as a temporary holding account for cash transactions
questionBank.exp: The Income Summary account is a temporary account used to summarize revenues and expenses during the closing process. The manual lists 'Close revenue accounts to income summary' and 'Close expense accounts to income summary' as steps in the closing process.

questionBank.q: Which of the following accounts would appear on the Statement of Financial Position at the end of the accounting period?
opts: Sales Revenue which represents income earned during the period
Rent Expense which represents costs incurred during the period
Accounts Payable which represents amounts owed to suppliers
Depreciation Expense which represents the period's depreciation charge
questionBank.exp: Accounts Payable is a liability account that appears on the Statement of Financial Position. Revenue and expense accounts are temporary accounts that are closed and do not appear on the Statement of Financial Position.

questionBank.q: When a company records a transaction in the general journal, what is the standard indentation convention?
opts: The debit account is indented and the credit account is written at the left margin
The credit account is indented and the debit account is written at the left margin
Both accounts are written at the left margin with the amount in separate columns
Accounts are written with no indentation, only the amounts are aligned
questionBank.exp: In standard journal entry format, the debit account is recorded first at the left margin, and the credit account is indented. The manual's examples show this formatting clearly.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a step in the closing process?
opts: Close revenue accounts to the Income Summary account
Close expense accounts to the Income Summary account
Close Income Summary to the Retained Earnings account
Close asset accounts to the Retained Earnings account
questionBank.exp: The manual lists the closing process steps as: Close revenue accounts to income summary, Close expense accounts to income summary, Close income summary to retained earnings, and Close dividends (or withdrawals) to retained earnings. Asset accounts are not closed.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance has total debits of N80,000 and total credits of N78,000. What can be concluded from these totals alone?
opts: Debits exceed credits by N2,000, but the totals alone do not identify the cause
A credit entry of N2,000 was definitely omitted
A debit entry of N2,000 was definitely omitted
A compensating error of exactly N2,000 definitely exists
questionBank.exp: The trial balance is out by N2,000, with debits exceeding credits. The totals show the size and direction of the difference, but do not by themselves establish which error caused it.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a purchase return in the accounting records?
opts: Debit Accounts Payable and Credit Purchases Returns for the amount returned
Credit Accounts Payable and Debit Purchases Returns for the amount returned
Debit Purchases and Credit Cash for the amount returned
Credit Purchases and Debit Cash for the amount returned
questionBank.exp: Returning goods purchased on credit reduces the liability (Accounts Payable, debit) and reduces the purchase amount (Purchases Returns, credit). The manual's transaction of returning goods to a supplier shows this treatment.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the post-closing trial balance in the accounting cycle?
opts: To verify that all temporary accounts have been closed to zero balance
To prepare the financial statements for the next accounting period
To identify errors that occurred during the closing process
To calculate the net profit for the next accounting period
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The post-closing trial balance is a list of balance sheet accounts with non-zero balances at the end of the reporting period.' It verifies that only permanent accounts remain with balances.

questionBank.q: Which account in the general ledger is most likely to have a debit balance?
opts: Accounts Payable which represents amounts owed to suppliers
Accumulated Depreciation which represents total depreciation taken
Prepaid Insurance which represents insurance paid in advance
Retained Earnings which represents accumulated profits retained
questionBank.exp: Prepaid Insurance is an asset account with a normal debit balance. Accounts Payable (liability), Accumulated Depreciation (contra-asset with credit balance), and Retained Earnings (equity with credit balance) have credit balances.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the Ledger in the accounting cycle?
opts: To provide a complete and cumulative record of each account's transactions and balance
To serve as the book of original entry where transactions are first recorded
To prepare the financial statements directly from the account balances
To record only the cash transactions of the business during the period
questionBank.exp: The ledger contains all accounts and provides a cumulative record of each account's transactions and current balance. The manual states: 'The general ledger contains a complete record of all accounts used by a company.'

questionBank.q: A company's Sales Ledger Control account shows a debit balance of N30,000. What does this balance represent?
opts: The total amount owed by the company to its suppliers
The total amount owed to the company by its credit customers
The total credit sales made by the company during the period
The total cash received from customers during the period
questionBank.exp: The Sales Ledger (or Accounts Receivable control account) has a debit balance representing the total amount owed to the company by its credit customers.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the 'Balance Off' process in ledger accounts?
opts: To calculate the debit or credit balance of each account at period end
To prepare the financial statements from the ledger balances
To ensure that all transactions have been recorded correctly
To close the ledger accounts at the end of the accounting period
questionBank.exp: 'Balancing off' a ledger account involves calculating the difference between total debits and total credits to determine the account's balance at the end of the period.

questionBank.q: A company has a debit balance of N4,000 in the Carriage Inwards account. How is this account treated in the financial statements?
opts: As an expense deducted from gross profit in the profit or loss account
As a cost added to purchases in the calculation of cost of sales
As a revenue item added to sales in the calculation of gross profit
As a liability on the Statement of Financial Position
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Carriage Inwards is an addition to the cost of purchases in the Trading Account.' It is added to purchases when calculating the cost of goods sold.

questionBank.q: When a company uses a control account for Accounts Receivable, what is the purpose of this control account?
opts: To provide a summary of all transactions with each individual customer
To provide the total balance of all Accounts Receivable in the general ledger
To replace the need for subsidiary ledgers for customer accounts
To record only the cash received from customers during the period
questionBank.exp: A control account provides a summary total for a group of accounts (like Accounts Receivable) in the general ledger. The individual details are maintained in subsidiary ledgers.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of a nominal account?
opts: Furniture and Fittings which represents a tangible asset
Accounts Receivable which represents amounts owed by customers
Sales Revenue which represents income earned by the business
Accounts Payable which represents amounts owed to suppliers
questionBank.exp: Nominal accounts are accounts that relate to income, expenses, gains, and losses. Sales Revenue is a nominal account. Assets (Furniture, Accounts Receivable) and Liabilities (Accounts Payable) are real accounts.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance shows a credit balance of N6,000 in the Provision for Depreciation account. What does this balance represent?
opts: The total depreciation expense for the current period
The cumulative depreciation charged on assets since acquisition
The amount set aside to replace assets in the future
The depreciation on assets sold during the current period
questionBank.exp: The Provision for Depreciation (Accumulated Depreciation) is a contra-asset account with a credit balance. It represents the total depreciation charged on assets since they were acquired.

questionBank.q: Which of the following transactions would be recorded in the General Journal rather than a specialized journal?
opts: Credit sales of goods to a customer for N1,500
Credit purchases of inventory from a supplier for N2,300
Depreciation adjustment for the year of N4,200
Cash receipt from a customer for N800
questionBank.exp: Depreciation is an adjusting entry that is not a routine cash or credit transaction. It would be recorded in the General Journal. The manual lists 'Adjustments to any of the entries in the ledgers' as a use of the General Journal.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of using subsidiary ledgers in conjunction with the general ledger?
opts: To provide detailed information that is not available in the general ledger control accounts
To replace the general ledger for all accounting transactions
To provide a complete record of all cash transactions only
To simplify the preparation of the financial statements
questionBank.exp: Subsidiary ledgers provide detailed breakdowns of the summary balances that appear in the general ledger's control accounts. For example, the Sales Ledger shows details of each customer's balance.

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance has a debit balance of N3,500 in the Cash account and a credit balance of N2,000 in the Bank Overdraft account. What do these balances indicate?
opts: The company has cash at bank and a positive cash balance
The company has N3,500 in cash and a N2,000 bank overdraft
The company has N5,500 in cash and no bank debt
The company has a net cash balance of N1,500
questionBank.exp: The Cash account with a debit balance indicates cash on hand. The Bank Overdraft account with a credit balance indicates the company owes the bank N2,000.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a transaction that requires a compound entry?
opts: The entry must include at least one debit and two credits or one credit and two debits
The entry must include only one debit and one credit for the entire transaction
The entry must include exactly two debits and two credits for the transaction
The entry must include more credits than debits for the transaction
questionBank.exp: A compound entry involves three or more accounts. It can have one debit and multiple credits, or one credit and multiple debits. The key requirement is that total debits equal total credits.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of preparing financial statements at the end of the accounting cycle?
opts: To calculate the income tax liability for the accounting period
To provide users with accurate information about the business's financial position and performance
To close the temporary accounts in preparation for the next accounting period
To verify the accuracy of the trial balance before the next period begins
questionBank.exp: Financial statements are the primary output of the accounting cycle. They provide stakeholders with information about the company's financial position, performance, and cash flows, which is essential for decision-making.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of preparing a bank reconciliation statement?
opts: To identify all cash transactions that occurred during the accounting period
To compare the company's accounting records with the bank statement and identify differences
To prepare the cash flow statement for the accounting period
To calculate the company's net profit or loss for the period
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Bank reconciliation is a financial process that compares a company's internal financial records with the records provided by its bank or financial institution. It is used to identify and resolve discrepancies.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following would cause the company's cash book balance to differ from the bank statement balance?
opts: The company records all cash receipts in its books immediately
The bank processes all transactions on the same day they occur
Outstanding checks that have been issued but not yet presented to the bank
The bank statement is prepared on the same date as the company's year-end
questionBank.exp: Outstanding checks (unpresented cheques) are a common reason for differences. The manual states: 'Unpresented cheques - Checks that have been issued by the company to creditors but have not been presented for payment.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as an unpresented cheque?
opts: A cheque received from a customer that has been deposited and cleared by the bank
A cheque issued by the company that has not yet been presented to the bank for payment
A cheque received from a customer that has been deposited but not yet credited by the bank
A cheque that was issued by the company and presented for payment
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Unpresented cheques / Outstanding checks: Checks that have been issued by the company to creditors but have not been presented for payment or the payments have not yet been processed.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be added to the balance per bank statement when reconciling?
opts: Unpresented cheques that have not yet cleared the bank
Uncredited cheques that have not yet been credited by the bank
Bank charges that were deducted by the bank
Dishonoured cheques returned by the bank
questionBank.exp: Uncredited cheques (deposits in transit) have been recorded by the company but not yet credited by the bank. They are added to the bank statement balance. The format shows: 'Less uncredited Cheques' when reconciling from the cash book balance.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be deducted from the balance per cash book when preparing a bank reconciliation?
opts: Unpresented cheques that have not yet cleared the bank
Uncredited cheques that have not yet been credited by the bank
Bank charges that were deducted by the bank but not recorded in the cash book
Direct deposits made by customers that were credited by the bank
questionBank.exp: Bank charges are deducted by the bank but may not yet be recorded in the company's cash book. They are deducted from the cash book balance when reconciling.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be added to the balance per cash book when preparing a bank reconciliation?
opts: Unpresented cheques that have not yet cleared the bank
Uncredited cheques that have not yet been credited by the bank
Bank charges that were deducted by the bank
Direct deposits (NIBSS credits) that were credited by the bank but not recorded in the cash book
questionBank.exp: Direct deposits or NIBSS credits are credited by the bank but may not yet be recorded in the company's cash book. They are added to the cash book balance when reconciling.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of a timing difference that causes the cash book and bank statement to differ?
opts: Bank charges that are deducted by the bank
The company recording an incorrect cheque amount in the cash book
A deposit in transit that has been recorded by the company but not by the bank
A dishonoured cheque that was returned by the bank
questionBank.exp: A deposit in transit is a timing difference because the company has recorded the deposit, but the bank has not yet processed and recorded it. The manual identifies uncredited cheques as a timing difference.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a dishonoured cheque in the bank reconciliation?
opts: Add it to the cash book balance because the bank has processed it
Deduct it from the cash book balance because the amount was not received
Add it to the bank statement balance because it represents a customer payment
Ignore it because it will be processed in the next period
questionBank.exp: A dishonoured cheque (bounced cheque) was previously recorded as a receipt in the cash book. When the bank returns it, the cash book must be adjusted by deducting the amount.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of preparing an adjusted cash book as part of the bank reconciliation process?
opts: To record all transactions that appear in the cash book but not in the bank statement
To update the cash book for transactions that appear in the bank statement but not in the cash book
To calculate the net profit or loss for the accounting period
To prepare the bank reconciliation statement directly
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Prepare the adjusted cash book by debiting it with all legitimate items credited in the bank statement and credit the cash book with all legitimate items debited in the bank statement.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for difference between the bank statement and the company's accounting records?
opts: Unpresented cheques that have been issued but not yet presented
Uncredited cheques that have been deposited but not yet credited
The company's accounting records are based on accrual accounting
Bank charges that have been deducted by the bank
questionBank.exp: Accrual accounting is a basis of accounting, not a reason for difference between the bank statement and cash book. The differences are caused by timing differences and items recorded by one party but not the other.

questionBank.q: What is a standing order in the context of bank reconciliation?
opts: A cheque that has been issued but not yet presented to the bank
A regular automatic payment set up by the account holder to pay a fixed amount
A deposit made by the company that has not yet been credited by the bank
A direct credit made by the bank to the company's account
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'A standing order is a financial arrangement that allows an account holder to set up automatic, recurring payments to be made from their bank account to another account on a fixed schedule.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a direct debit in the bank reconciliation?
opts: Add it to the cash book balance because the bank has debited the account
Deduct it from the cash book balance because the bank has made a payment on behalf of the company
Add it to the bank statement balance because it represents a bank charge
Ignore it until the company receives notification from the bank
questionBank.exp: A direct debit is a payment made automatically from the company's bank account. The bank records it on the bank statement, but it may not yet be recorded in the cash book. It should be deducted from the cash book balance.

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a debit balance of N15,000. The bank statement shows a credit balance of N18,000. Which of the following is a possible explanation for the difference?
opts: The company has unpresented cheques of N3,000 that have not yet been cleared
The company has uncredited cheques of N3,000 that have not yet been credited by the bank
The bank has deducted N3,000 in charges that were not recorded in the cash book
The company has not recorded a N3,000 direct deposit from a customer
questionBank.exp: If the cash book balance is lower than the bank statement balance (N15,000 vs N18,000), the company must have issued cheques that haven't been presented (unpresented cheques). These reduce the cash book balance but the bank doesn't know about them yet.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would NOT appear on a bank reconciliation statement?
opts: Unpresented cheques that have been issued but not yet presented
Uncredited cheques that have been deposited but not yet credited
Bank charges that have been deducted but not yet recorded in the cash book
Depreciation expense for the accounting period
questionBank.exp: Depreciation expense is a non-cash item that does not affect the bank account. It would not appear on a bank reconciliation statement, which only deals with cash and bank transactions.

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a cheque issued to a supplier that remains unpresented at the end of the accounting period?
opts: Deduct it from the bank statement balance in the reconciliation statement
Add it to the bank statement balance in the reconciliation statement
Deduct it from the cash book balance in the reconciliation statement
No adjustment is required because it is a timing difference
questionBank.exp: Unpresented cheques have been recorded in the cash book (reducing the balance) but not yet processed by the bank. When reconciling from the bank statement balance, unpresented cheques are deducted.

questionBank.q: A company's bank reconciliation shows a difference of N2,000. After investigation, it is found that the bank had incorrectly debited the company's account. What is the correct treatment?
opts: Adjust the cash book balance by adding N2,000
Adjust the cash book balance by deducting N2,000
Contact the bank to correct the error and not adjust the cash book
Adjust the bank statement balance by adding N2,000
questionBank.exp: If the bank has made an error, the correction should be made by the bank. The company should contact the bank to correct the error rather than adjusting the cash book. However, in the reconciliation, the error would appear as an 'other error' in the bank.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct format for a bank reconciliation statement when starting from the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: Adjusted Cash Book Balance + Unpresented Cheques - Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
Adjusted Cash Book Balance - Unpresented Cheques + Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
Adjusted Cash Book Balance + Unpresented Cheques + Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
Adjusted Cash Book Balance - Unpresented Cheques - Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
questionBank.exp: The manual shows the format: 'Balance as per adjusted Cash Book + Add Unpresented Cheques - Less uncredited Cheques = Balance as per Bank Statement.'

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a balance of N20,000. The bank statement shows a balance of N18,000. The difference is a N2,000 cheque issued to a supplier that has not yet been presented. What is the correct reconciliation?
opts: Cash Book N20,000 - Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Bank Statement N18,000
Cash Book N20,000 + Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Bank Statement N22,000
Bank Statement N18,000 + Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Cash Book N20,000
Bank Statement N18,000 - Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Cash Book N16,000
questionBank.exp: The company has recorded the payment in the cash book (N20,000), but the bank hasn't processed it yet, so the bank balance is higher (N18,000). The unpresented cheque of N2,000 is deducted from the cash book balance to arrive at the bank statement balance: N20,000 - N2,000 = N18,000.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a reason for preparing bank reconciliation statements regularly?
opts: To identify cash transactions that have been recorded in error
To ensure all deposits and withdrawals are accurately recorded
To detect fraud and unauthorized transactions
All of the above
questionBank.exp: The manual states the importance of bank reconciliation includes: 'Accuracy Assurance: ensures company's cash balance matches actual bank balance,' 'Fraud Detection: can help detect unauthorized transactions,' and 'Error Identification: discrepancies may highlight errors.'

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a NIBSS credit in the bank reconciliation?
opts: Add it to the cash book balance because it is a direct deposit to the company's account
Deduct it from the cash book balance because it is a bank fee
Add it to the bank statement balance because it is a timing difference
Ignore it because it is not a cash transaction
questionBank.exp: A NIBSS credit (direct deposit) is credited by the bank but may not yet be recorded in the cash book. It should be added to the cash book balance. The manual's example shows a 'NIBSS Credit 24' in the bank statement that needs to be recorded in the cash book.

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a balance of N30,000. Bank charges of N400 and direct deposit of N2,000 appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: N32,400 which is the cash book balance plus direct deposit less bank charges
N31,600 which is the cash book balance plus direct deposit less bank charges
N30,000 which is the cash book balance unchanged by these items
N32,400 which is the cash book balance plus bank charges less direct deposit
questionBank.exp: Adjusted cash book = N30,000 + N2,000 (direct deposit) - N400 (bank charges) = N31,600.

questionBank.q: Which of the following errors would cause the cash book balance to be overstated?
opts: A cheque issued to a supplier was recorded as N5,000 instead of N500 in the cash book
A cheque received from a customer was recorded as N500 instead of N5,000 in the cash book
Bank charges were recorded as income instead of expenses in the cash book
A direct deposit from a customer was not recorded in the cash book
questionBank.exp: If a cheque received from a customer was recorded as N5,000 instead of the actual N500, the cash book balance would be overstated by N4,500.

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a cheque that was deposited by the company but was returned by the bank as dishonoured?
opts: Deduct the cheque amount from the cash book balance
Add the cheque amount to the cash book balance
Deduct the cheque amount from the bank statement balance
Add the cheque amount to the bank statement balance
questionBank.exp: A dishonoured cheque was previously recorded as a receipt in the cash book. When the bank returns it, the cash book must be adjusted by deducting the amount. The manual identifies 'Dishonoured Cheques' as a reason for difference.

questionBank.q: A company has unpresented cheques of N8,000 and uncredited cheques of N5,000. The bank statement shows a balance of N25,000. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: N22,000 which is the bank balance plus unpresented less uncredited
N20,000 which is the bank balance plus uncredited less unpresented
N28,000 which is the bank balance plus uncredited and unpresented
N30,000 which is the bank balance plus unpresented and uncredited
questionBank.exp: Adjusted Cash Book = Bank Statement - Unpresented + Uncredited = N25,000 - N8,000 + N5,000 = N22,000.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence for preparing a bank reconciliation?
opts: Prepare bank reconciliation statement directly from cash book and bank statement
Prepare adjusted cash book, then bank reconciliation statement
Prepare bank statement first, then adjusted cash book, then reconciliation
Prepare adjusted cash book and bank reconciliation statement simultaneously
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'a. Prepare the adjusted cash book by debiting it with all legitimate items credited in the bank statement and credit the cash book with all legitimate items debited in the bank statement. b. Prepare the Bank Reconciliation Statement.'

questionBank.q: When a customer deposits N100,000 into their current account, what is the correct accounting entry for the bank?
opts: Debit Cash Account and Credit Customer's Current Account for the full deposit amount
Credit Cash Account and Debit Customer's Current Account for the full deposit amount
Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Loan Account for the full deposit amount
Credit Customer's Current Account and Debit Interest Income for the full deposit amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When a customer deposits N100,000 in a current account: Dr: Cash Account (Asset) N100,000, Cr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N100,000.' Deposits are liabilities for the bank.

questionBank.q: When a bank originates a N1,200,000 loan to a customer, what is the correct accounting entry?
opts: Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the loan amount
Debit Customer's Loan Receivable Account and Credit Customer's Current Account for the loan amount
Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the loan disbursement
Debit Interest Income and Credit Customer's Current Account for the loan amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank originates a N1,200,000 loan... Dr: Customer's Loan Receivable Account (Asset) N1,200,000, Cr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N1,200,000.'

questionBank.q: A customer makes a loan repayment of N115,000 which includes N100,000 principal and N15,000 interest. What is the correct journal entry?
opts: Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the full amount
Debit Customer's Current Account, Credit Customer's Loan Receivable N100,000, and Credit Interest Income N15,000
Debit Customer's Loan Receivable Account and Credit Interest Income for the full amount
Debit Interest Income and Credit Customer's Current Account for the full repayment amount
questionBank.exp: The manual shows: 'When the customer makes a repayment of N115,000... Dr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N115,000, Cr: Customer's Loan Receivable Account (Asset) N100,000, Cr: Interest Income (Revenue) N15,000.'

questionBank.q: When a bank purchases N50,000,000 in government bonds, what is the correct accounting entry?
opts: Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit Bank's CBN Operating Account for the purchase amount
Credit Investment in Government Bonds and Debit Bank's CBN Operating Account for the purchase amount
Debit Cash and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the bond purchase
Credit Investment in Government Bonds and Debit Interest Income for the bond purchase
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank purchases N50,000,000 worth of government bonds: Dr: Investment in Government Bonds (Asset) N50,000,000, Cr: Bank's CBN Operating Account (Asset) N50,000,000.'

questionBank.q: When a customer purchases a N500,000 Certificate of Deposit, what is the correct accounting entry for the bank?
opts: Debit Certificate of Deposit and Credit Customer's Current Account for the CD purchase
Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Certificate of Deposit for the CD purchase
Debit Certificate of Deposit and Credit Interest Income for the CD purchase
Debit Cash and Credit Certificate of Deposit for the CD purchase
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When a customer purchases a N500,000 CD: Dr: Customer's Current/Savings Account (Liability) N500,000, Cr: Certificate of Deposit (Liability) N500,000.'

questionBank.q: A bank sells government bonds for N50,050,000 when the carrying amount is N50,000,000. What is the correct journal entry?
opts: Debit CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, and Credit Realized Gain N50,000
Credit CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Debit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, and Debit Realized Gain N50,000
Debit CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,050,000, and Credit Realized Gain N50,000
Debit CBN Operating Account N50,000,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,050,000, and Debit Realized Loss N50,000
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank sells the investments for proceeds of N50,050,000... Dr: CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Cr: Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, Cr: Realized Gain Account N50,000.'

questionBank.q: A bank sells government bonds for N49,975,000 when the carrying amount is N50,000,000. What is the correct journal entry?
opts: Debit CBN Operating Account N50,000,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N49,975,000, and Credit Realized Gain N25,000
Debit CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Debit Realized Loss N25,000, and Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000
Credit CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Credit Realized Loss N25,000, and Debit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000
Debit CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, and Credit Realized Gain N25,000
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank sells the investments for proceeds of N49,975,000... Dr: CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Dr: Realized Loss N25,000, Cr: Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000.'

questionBank.q: When a bank sets aside a N100,000,000 provision for loan losses, what is the correct accounting entry?
opts: Debit Loan Loss Reserves and Credit Loan Loss Expense for the provision amount
Debit Loan Loss Expense and Credit Loan Loss Reserves for the provision amount
Debit Cash and Credit Loan Loss Reserves for the provision amount
Debit Loan Loss Expense and Credit Cash for the provision amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank sets aside a N100,000,000 as loan loss provision: Dr: Loan Loss Expense (Income Statement) N100,000,000, Cr: Loan Loss Reserves (Contra Asset) N100,000,000.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the role of accounting in ensuring regulatory compliance for banks?
opts: Accounting helps banks avoid paying taxes by minimizing reported income
Accounting enables banks to measure capital adequacy and meet Basel III reporting requirements
Accounting allows banks to delay the recognition of losses for regulatory purposes
Accounting ensures that banks can maximize their profits by choosing favorable accounting methods
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Accounting standards are essential for meeting regulatory requirements, such as those set forth by Basel III. Banks must maintain sufficient capital reserves, and accurate accounting is crucial for measuring capital adequacy.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct entry when a customer withdraws N50,000 by writing a cheque?
opts: Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Current Account for the withdrawal amount
Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Cash for the withdrawal amount
Debit Customer's Loan Account and Credit Cash for the withdrawal amount
Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Loan Account for the withdrawal amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When a customer writes a check for N50,000: Dr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N50,000, Cr: Cash (Asset) N50,000.'

questionBank.q: When a CD matures and the bank pays the customer N525,000 (N500,000 principal plus N25,000 interest), what is the correct journal entry?
opts: Debit Certificate of Deposit N525,000 and Credit Cash N525,000 for the full payment
Debit Certificate of Deposit N500,000, Debit Interest Expense N25,000, and Credit Cash N525,000
Debit Cash N525,000, Credit Certificate of Deposit N500,000, and Credit Interest Income N25,000
Debit Interest Expense N25,000 and Credit Certificate of Deposit N500,000 for the full payment
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the CD matures and the bank pays the customer N525,000... Dr: Certificate of Deposit (Liability) N500,000, Dr: Interest Expense (Expense) N25,000, Cr: Cash/CBN Operating Account (Asset) N525,000.'

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of the Loan Loss Reserves account in banking?
opts: To record the actual losses from loans that have been written off as uncollectible
To provide a cushion for expected future loan defaults based on historical experience
To set aside cash for dividend payments to shareholders
To reduce the bank's tax liability by recognizing expenses
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Banks must set aside provisions for loan losses to account for potential defaults on loans. This is an accounting expense that reduces net income.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways accounting supports decision-making in banking?
opts: Performance analysis through ratios like ROA and ROE
Budgeting and forecasting based on historical financial records
Risk management through stress testing and scenario analysis
Determining employee salaries and compensation packages
questionBank.exp: The manual lists performance analysis, budgeting and forecasting, and risk management as ways accounting supports decision-making. Employee compensation is not identified as a primary accounting function in banking.

questionBank.q: When a bank receives N10,000 in interest income from its investments, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: Debit Interest Income and Credit Bank's CBN Operating Account for the interest received
Debit Bank's CBN Operating Account and Credit Interest Income for the interest received
Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit Interest Income for the interest received
Debit Cash and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the interest received
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank receives N10,000 in interest income from its investments: Dr: Bank's CBN Operating Account (Asset) N10,000, Cr: Interest Income (Income Statement) N10,000.'

questionBank.q: When investments mature and the bank receives N50,000,000, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit CBN Operating Account for the maturity amount
Debit CBN Operating Account and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the maturity amount
Debit Cash and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the maturity amount
Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit Interest Income for the maturity amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the investments mature: Dr: CBN Operating Account (Asset) N50,000,000, Cr: Investment in Government Bonds (Asset) N50,000,000.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following describes how accounting helps banks detect money laundering and fraud?
opts: Accounting eliminates the need for Know Your Customer procedures
Accounting helps banks monitor account activity and identify unusual patterns
Accounting allows banks to avoid reporting suspicious transactions
Accounting ensures that all customer transactions are approved by management
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Accounting helps banks detect suspicious transactions and comply with AML regulations. Banks monitor account activity and use accounting data to identify unusual patterns.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a bank's customer deposits in the context of the accounting equation?
opts: Deposits are assets because they represent cash held by the bank
Deposits are liabilities because the bank owes the deposited funds to customers
Deposits are equity because they represent ownership in the bank
Deposits are revenue because they generate fee income for the bank
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When customers deposit funds into their bank accounts... banks must record these deposits as liabilities because they owe the deposited amount to the customers.'

questionBank.q: What is the role of accounting in asset and liability management for banks?
opts: To ensure that the bank can meet its obligations to depositors while generating income from assets
To maximize the bank's profits by investing in high-risk assets
To reduce the bank's liabilities by encouraging customers to withdraw deposits
To ensure that all bank assets are fully insured by the government
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Banks rely on accounting to manage assets and liabilities effectively. Accurate records facilitate asset and liability matching, ensuring that the bank can meet its obligations to depositors while generating income from its assets.'

questionBank.q: When a bank originates a loan, how is the loan classified on the bank's Statement of Financial Position?
opts: As a liability because the bank will receive future cash flows from the customer
As an asset because it represents a future economic benefit from the customer's repayments
As equity because the loan increases the bank's capital base
As revenue because the loan generates interest income for the bank
questionBank.exp: A loan receivable is an asset for the bank because it represents the right to receive future cash flows from the borrower.

questionBank.q: What is the effect on the bank's accounting equation when a customer deposits N50,000 into a savings account?
opts: Assets increase by N50,000 and liabilities increase by N50,000
Assets decrease by N50,000 and liabilities decrease by N50,000
Assets increase by N50,000 and equity increase by N50,000
Liabilities increase by N50,000 and equity decrease by N50,000
questionBank.exp: The bank receives cash (asset increases) and creates a deposit liability (liability increases). Equity remains unchanged.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between accounting and risk management in banking?
opts: Accounting is primarily used to hide risk from regulators and investors
Accounting provides data that helps banks identify, measure, and manage financial risks
Accounting eliminates all operational risks in banking operations
Accounting is only relevant for historical reporting, not future risk management
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Accounting plays a crucial role in risk assessment and management. Banks use accounting data to identify credit, liquidity, and operational risks.'

questionBank.q: Why may an error of omission remain undetected by a trial balance?
opts: Because the transaction was not recorded, so the debit and credit totals may still agree
Because it always causes unequal debit and credit totals
Because it can occur only in the General Journal
Because it automatically creates a suspense-account entry
questionBank.exp: The Retail manual explains that an error of omission occurs when no entry for a transaction has been made, and that a trial balance does not reveal all types of errors.

questionBank.q: What does a credit balance in a Bank account generally indicate in the trial balance?
opts: A positive cash asset balance
A bank overdraft, which is a liability
An account that can never be reconciled
An automatic transfer to the suspense account
questionBank.exp: The Retail manual lists a bank overdraft as a liability. A credit balance in the Bank account generally indicates an overdraft rather than a positive cash-at-bank asset balance.

questionBank.q: Why might a business prefer to record routine credit sales in a Sales Journal rather than the General Journal?
opts: Because the Sales Journal allows similar high-volume transactions to be grouped and processed efficiently
Because the General Journal cannot legally be used to record any form of revenue transaction
Because the Sales Journal eliminates the need to ever post entries to the general ledger
Because credit sales must always bypass the journal stage and go directly to the ledger
questionBank.exp: Specialized journals like the Sales Journal allow businesses to group and process high-volume, similar transactions efficiently, rather than recording each individually in the General Journal.

questionBank.q: According to the Retail manual, which types of accounts are contained in the General Ledger?
opts: Personal accounts of credit customers only
Personal accounts of credit suppliers only
Real and nominal accounts, including accounts for non-current assets, expenses, cash and capital
Only temporary income and expense accounts that are closed at year-end
questionBank.exp: The manual states that the General Ledger contains the Real Accounts and Nominal Accounts, including accounts relating to non-current assets, expenses, cash and capital.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly explains why a Suspense Account is considered a temporary, not permanent, solution to a trial balance imbalance?
opts: Because it permanently absorbs any unresolved differences without further investigation
Because it is only used until the underlying error causing the imbalance is identified and corrected
Because it is automatically closed to the General Journal at the end of each financial year
Because it replaces the need to ever balance debits and credits again going forward
questionBank.exp: A Suspense Account is a temporary holding account used only until the discrepancy causing the trial balance imbalance is identified and properly corrected.

questionBank.q: Why is 'carriage outwards' treated differently from 'carriage inwards' in the preparation of financial statements?
opts: Because carriage outwards is added to purchases, while carriage inwards is a selling expense
Because carriage inwards is added to the cost of purchases, while carriage outwards is a selling and distribution expense
Because carriage inwards and carriage outwards are always treated identically as cost of sales items
Because carriage outwards is treated as a non-current asset on the Statement of Financial Position
questionBank.exp: Carriage inwards is added to the cost of purchases in calculating cost of sales, while carriage outwards is treated as a selling and distribution expense in the profit or loss account.

questionBank.q: Why can a company's cash book balance and its bank statement balance legitimately differ even when no errors have been made by either party?
opts: Because timing differences arise from items recorded by one party before the other processes them
Because the bank is legally permitted to record transactions inaccurately without correction
Because the company is required to record all transactions a full month after they occur
Because bank statements are only issued once every six months under standard banking practice
questionBank.exp: Timing differences, such as unpresented or uncredited cheques, naturally arise because one party (the company or the bank) may record a transaction before the other has processed it.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best distinguishes an 'unpresented cheque' from an 'uncredited cheque'?
opts: An unpresented cheque is issued by the company and not yet cleared; an uncredited cheque is received by the company and not yet credited by the bank
An unpresented cheque is received by the company; an uncredited cheque is issued by the company
Both terms describe the exact same type of timing difference between cash book and bank statement
An unpresented cheque relates only to standing orders, while an uncredited cheque relates only to direct debits
questionBank.exp: An unpresented cheque is one the company has issued to a payee but which has not yet cleared the bank, while an uncredited cheque is one the company has received and recorded but the bank has not yet credited.

questionBank.q: Why is it important for a business to perform bank reconciliations on a regular basis rather than only at year-end?
opts: Because regular reconciliation helps detect fraud and errors promptly rather than allowing them to accumulate
Because banks legally require reconciliation to be performed daily for every business account
Because year-end reconciliation is prohibited under standard accounting practice
Because regular reconciliation eliminates the need to ever prepare a cash book
questionBank.exp: Performing bank reconciliations regularly, rather than only at year-end, helps a business detect fraud, unauthorized transactions, and errors promptly rather than allowing them to accumulate undetected.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would require an adjustment to the cash book balance, rather than the bank statement balance, during reconciliation?
opts: A cheque issued by the company that has not yet been presented to the bank for payment
A bank charge deducted by the bank that has not yet been recorded in the company's cash book
A deposit recorded by the company that has not yet been credited by the bank
Both unpresented and uncredited cheques, since these always adjust the bank statement balance
questionBank.exp: Bank charges are deducted by the bank but typically are not yet known to or recorded by the company, so they require an adjustment to the cash book balance to bring it up to date.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains the purpose of preparing an adjusted cash book before drawing up the bank reconciliation statement?
opts: To update the company's own records for legitimate items appearing on the bank statement but not yet recorded internally
To eliminate the need to compare the cash book and bank statement at all
To transfer all uncredited cheques permanently into the unpresented cheques category
To ensure the bank statement balance is changed to match the cash book exactly
questionBank.exp: The adjusted cash book updates the company's own records to reflect legitimate items, such as bank charges, direct debits, or interest, that appear on the bank statement but have not yet been recorded internally.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly explains why interest earned on a bank balance typically requires an adjustment to the company's cash book?
opts: Because the bank credits the interest directly to the account, and the company may not yet have recorded this income
Because interest earned is always recorded by the company before the bank processes it
Because interest income is treated as a liability rather than an asset on the company's books
Because interest earned is excluded entirely from any bank reconciliation statement
questionBank.exp: The bank credits interest earned directly to the account, and the company typically only becomes aware of and records this income once the bank statement is reviewed, requiring a cash book adjustment.

questionBank.q: Why might a business reconciling its bank account discover an error made by the bank itself rather than by the company?
opts: Because banks occasionally make processing errors, which the reconciliation process is designed to help uncover
Because banks are never responsible for verifying the accuracy of their own statements
Because bank errors are automatically corrected without the need for any reconciliation process
Because companies are legally prohibited from contacting their bank about statement discrepancies
questionBank.exp: Occasionally, the bank itself may make errors in its statements or transactions, and the reconciliation process is specifically designed to help uncover such discrepancies for correction.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes why direct credits and direct debits often appear on the bank statement before they appear in the company's cash book?
opts: Because these electronic transfers are processed automatically by the bank, often before the company becomes aware of them
Because direct credits and debits are recorded by the company well before the bank ever processes them
Because electronic transfers are not permitted to be recorded in the cash book at all
Because direct credits and debits are reserved exclusively for international transactions
questionBank.exp: Direct credits and debits are electronic funds transfers processed automatically by the bank, often before the company becomes aware of them and records them in its own cash book.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would NOT typically require any adjustment during a bank reconciliation process?
opts: A cheque issued by the company that has already been presented and cleared by the bank
A cheque issued by the company that remains outstanding at the bank
A deposit recorded by the company that the bank has not yet credited
Bank charges that have been deducted by the bank but not yet recorded by the company
questionBank.exp: A cheque that has already cleared the bank is reflected identically in both the cash book and bank statement, so it requires no further reconciling adjustment, unlike outstanding or uncredited items.

questionBank.q: Why would a company's cash book understate its true cash position if it failed to record a direct credit received from a customer?
opts: Because the bank has already recorded the increase in funds, but the company's own books do not yet reflect it
Because direct credits always reduce the company's recorded cash balance rather than increasing it
Because direct credits are recorded only in the Purchases Journal, not the cash book
Because the company's bank statement would also fail to show the direct credit until reconciliation
questionBank.exp: If a direct credit from a customer is not yet recorded by the company, the bank statement already reflects the increased funds while the cash book understates the company's true cash position.

questionBank.q: Why might bank charges deducted automatically by the bank still need to be reflected in the company's adjusted cash book?
opts: Because they represent a genuine reduction in the company's true cash position that must be recorded
Because bank charges are always reversed by the bank once a reconciliation is completed
Because bank charges are classified as a non-cash item and therefore excluded from reconciliation entirely
Because companies are never permitted to record any expense charged directly by a bank
questionBank.exp: Bank charges represent a genuine reduction in the company's actual cash position, so they must be recorded in the adjusted cash book to reflect the company's true, up-to-date cash balance.

questionBank.q: Why is it inaccurate to assume that a difference between the cash book and bank statement always indicates an error by either party?
opts: Because many differences are simply timing differences from legitimate transactions not yet processed by both parties
Because cash book and bank statement balances are required by law to always match exactly
Because timing differences are eliminated entirely once a company adopts accrual accounting
Because only fraudulent transactions can cause any difference between the two balances
questionBank.exp: Many differences between the cash book and bank statement are simply legitimate timing differences, such as unpresented or uncredited cheques, rather than indicating an actual error by either party.

questionBank.q: Why are customer deposits recorded as a liability on a bank's books rather than as revenue or equity?
opts: Because the bank owes the deposited funds back to the customer upon demand or at maturity
Because customer deposits represent the bank's own capital contribution to its operations
Because customer deposits are treated as income earned by the bank from its customers
Because customer deposits are classified as a non-current asset on the bank's records
questionBank.exp: Customer deposits are recorded as a liability because the bank owes the deposited amount back to the customer, rather than the funds being income or capital belonging to the bank itself.

questionBank.q: Why does a bank record a loan disbursed to a customer as an asset rather than an expense?
opts: Because the loan represents a future economic benefit in the form of expected repayments and interest from the customer
Because loans disbursed are always immediately converted into the bank's own equity
Because the bank expects no future repayment once a loan has been disbursed to a customer
Because loans are treated as a direct reduction in the bank's reported revenue for the period
questionBank.exp: A loan disbursed to a customer is recorded as an asset because it represents the bank's right to receive future repayments of principal and interest from the borrower.

questionBank.q: Why would a Certificate of Deposit (CD) be recorded as a liability for the issuing bank?
opts: Because the bank has an obligation to repay the customer the deposited amount, typically with interest, at maturity
Because a CD represents an investment the bank itself has made in another financial institution
Because a CD is treated as part of the bank's own retained earnings until it matures
Because a CD generates no future obligation for the bank once it has been issued
questionBank.exp: A CD is recorded as a liability because the bank has an obligation to repay the customer the principal, typically along with interest, once the CD reaches maturity.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why a bank recognizes a realized gain when it sells an investment security above its carrying amount?
opts: Because the sale proceeds exceed the recorded book value of the investment, generating a profit on disposal
Because realized gains only occur when an investment security is purchased, not sold
Because the bank automatically records a gain whenever any investment matures, regardless of price
Because realized gains are recorded as a liability rather than as income for the period
questionBank.exp: A realized gain arises because the sale proceeds exceed the carrying amount (book value) of the investment, representing a profit recognized at the point of disposal.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why accounting is described as essential to a bank's asset and liability management?
opts: Because accurate records allow the bank to match its assets and liabilities effectively, ensuring it can meet obligations to depositors
Because accounting eliminates the need for banks to ever hold any liquid assets at all
Because asset and liability management is solely the responsibility of bank regulators, not accountants
Because accounting only tracks a bank's liabilities, leaving asset management to a separate department
questionBank.exp: Accurate accounting records allow a bank to effectively match its assets, such as loans, against its liabilities, such as deposits, ensuring it can meet its obligations to depositors while generating income.

questionBank.q: Why might a bank's use of accounting ratios, such as Return on Assets (ROA), be particularly important for performance analysis?
opts: Because such ratios allow the bank to gauge profitability and efficiency using standardized accounting data
Because ROA is the only ratio banks are permitted to disclose to regulators
Because accounting ratios eliminate the need for any further risk assessment by the bank
Because ROA measures only a bank's total liabilities rather than its overall performance
questionBank.exp: Ratios like Return on Assets allow a bank to gauge its profitability and efficiency using standardized accounting data, supporting meaningful performance analysis and benchmarking.

questionBank.q: Why does Basel III specifically require banks to maintain accurate accounting records related to capital adequacy?
opts: Because accurate accounting is crucial for measuring whether a bank holds sufficient capital reserves as required by regulation
Because Basel III only applies to the marketing and sales departments of a bank
Because capital adequacy measurement is entirely unrelated to a bank's accounting function
Because Basel III eliminates the need for banks to report any balance sheet information
questionBank.exp: Basel III requires banks to maintain sufficient capital reserves, and accurate accounting is essential for measuring whether a bank's capital adequacy meets these regulatory requirements.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why a bank's accounting function supports effective budgeting and forecasting?
opts: Because historical financial records provide the basis for projecting future revenues, expenses, and cash flows
Because budgeting and forecasting are entirely unrelated to a bank's accounting records
Because accounting data is only useful for satisfying external regulatory reporting requirements
Because forecasts are generated independently of any accounting information held by the bank
questionBank.exp: Accounting data provides the historical financial records that form the basis for a bank's budgeting and forecasting processes, supporting projections of future revenues, expenses, and cash flows.

questionBank.q: Why might stress testing and scenario analysis in banking rely heavily on accounting information?
opts: Because accounting data allows banks to evaluate their resilience to adverse economic conditions based on actual financial positions
Because stress testing is performed exclusively using data unrelated to a bank's financial records
Because scenario analysis eliminates the need for any accounting-based risk assessment
Because stress testing only applies to a bank's marketing and customer service functions
questionBank.exp: Stress testing and scenario analysis rely on accounting information because they evaluate a bank's resilience to adverse economic conditions based on its actual recorded financial position.

questionBank.q: Why is the recognition of realized gains and losses on investment securities important for a bank's financial reporting?
opts: Because it accurately reflects the actual financial outcome of disposing of an investment relative to its recorded carrying value
Because realized gains and losses are excluded entirely from a bank's income statement
Because investment securities are never disposed of by banks under standard practice
Because realized gains and losses only affect a bank's liabilities, not its overall profitability
questionBank.exp: Recognizing realized gains and losses ensures that a bank's financial statements accurately reflect the actual financial outcome of disposing of an investment compared to its recorded carrying value.

questionBank.q: Why does the manual describe accounting as playing a 'multifaceted' role in the banking sector?
opts: Because accounting simultaneously supports accurate record-keeping, informed decision-making, and regulatory compliance within banks
Because accounting in banking is limited solely to the preparation of tax returns each year
Because accounting only affects a bank's marketing strategy, with no broader organizational impact
Because the role of accounting in banking has remained completely unchanged over time
questionBank.exp: Accounting is described as multifaceted in banking because it simultaneously supports accurate record-keeping, informed decision-making, and adherence to regulatory compliance requirements.
